utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. But I must point out to the technicians and the translators that there is no reflection, no replication of what the accused said in the transcript, and I did not hear or receive any interpretation myself in English, although I am on channel 4. Of course I can repeat it, but just for the record I needed to point this out. So I'm sorry, Mr. Oric. Unfortunately, there was a technical hitch. I have to ask you again: Are you receiving interpretation in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Appearances. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution team, together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink; and also good morning to the Defence team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, together with Mr. John Jones, appearing for the Defence Mr. Naser Oric. With us today are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two limited issues. One will be raised by Ms. Patricia Sellers and by me, referring to the witness schedule of 11th of January, please be informed that the witness on that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean 11th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: 11th of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I understand you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dated the 11th of January, Your Honour - I'm sorry I was not explicit enough - but that schedule projected a witness on the 18th of January only limited to two hours. That witness is cancelled due to the changes of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why? Did you take note of that, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I did. Unfortunately, I don't have the schedule here. If Mr. Wubben could just tell us the name of that witness. I do not believe that it is a protected witness anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will write down the name on a note, if the Defence counsel allow me, and ask the usher to pass it to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, there's no indication here whether he is a protected witness or not. Otherwise, there is another issue you would like to raise Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's just to inform the Trial Chamber, Defence counsel and Prosecution, we believe we've reached substantial agreement in terms of the 94 bis filing as it points to the possibility of having filed quite a few pages that had -- would have had to have been translated that dealt with autopsy reports that are not the underlying substantiation of any deaths in our indictment as charged, we'd like to inform the Trial Chamber that we will be filing a 94 bis motion this afternoon as it relates to one of the underlying crime base persons, and that's Mr. Kostadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the rest can be filed in person by the expert himself while he's here giving testimony. That's so simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe at that point 94 bis rules will apply the Defence will indicate whether they will accept the report as filed or whether they wish to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you would cooperate on this. It shouldn't be a bone of contention between you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why we've been in discussions with the Prosecution. There are concerns, serious concerns we have that Dr. Stankovic, if he came here and gave evidence orally, would embark on an inquest into all sorts of deaths, dozens of deaths in Kravica, Fakovici, Rakovici, and we're completely opposed to that because we've never cross-examined on cause of death so part of our operation is we -- under no circumstances do we want Dr. Stankovic to come here and give that evidence so we're seeking to find common ground with the Prosecution as regards the autopsy of Kostadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll file a response setting out our position, but we are, of course, being as cooperative as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I understand that. Okay, thank you, Mr. Jones. Anything else? So Madam Usher, could please escort the witness in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Radic. We are going to proceed, to continue and hopefully finish with your cross-examination. We should finish before the end of the morning. That doesn't depend on me, or us; it depends on you and also on Mr. Jones. I hope you had a restful weekend and that you are feeling somewhat better. If at any time you are not feeling well, please, like last time, do draw my attention to it. I will discuss it with the two Judges and we will take a decision, and of course the decision will take into consideration your situation. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just remind you that you are still testifying under the solemn declaration that you made last week that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm here to do, Your Honours. I think so far I have complied in full with these obligations that I undertook. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Radic. Yes, Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May it please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I too hope that you're feeling better this morning.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much better. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now on Friday when we had to break off, I was asking you about your purported identification of Naser Oric after you left the prison from a videotape and then from a TV broadcast of these proceedings. So I'm going to ask you a couple of more questions on that subject before moving on to another area. And first I want to make clear, really in order to save time more than anything, that I'm not asking you to state how positive you are about your identification. You told us you're a hundred per cent sure, but with respect, you might be a hundred per cent wrong. So what I'm asking you is about specific physical features which can be verified because I take it you agree that human faces are similar, that many people resemble other people, if that's clear. Now, in summary, am I right then in saying that there's no feature about Mr. Oric's face that you can point to and say, "That's what I recognise"? And if there is such a feature, please let us know specifically what it was.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can explain this in the following way: Following my exchange, when I saw that gentleman on horseback, my conclusion was that it was Mr. Naser Oric. I may be mistaken, but I do feel 100 per cent certain. I have a photograph from Friday's newspaper, Mr. Naser Oric with a beard. I did not want to bring it along. Also, when he entered a plea before this Tribunal, I saw him again. I don't think I could go wrong there, but then again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm coming to the court appearance in a moment. We're still on the video. You referred on Friday to the hair of the person on the horseback and you said -- you described, firstly, the person you saw in the prison as being "clean-shaven with a crewcut, short hair." And then from the video you said, "His hair changed a bit. He was -- he had a short haircut at the time." So my question is: Was this a crewcut; short all round, short back, short sides, short at the top? Is that what -- is that the hairstyle which you saw in the prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the haircut on when he was on horseback or what his hair was like. I knew that he had a beard, which was not the case in the prison. He had very short hair when he came to see us. But when I saw him on horseback, I can't remember exactly what his hair was like, therefore, I don't think I'm able to answer that question. It's better that I remain silent on the issue rather than say something that may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, as far as the video is concerned, I think you said you saw it maybe one or two years after your capture. I would suggest to you that in fact that video wasn't circulated until after the fall of Srebrenica, that is July 1995, when the tape was seized by the Serbs. So my question is: Would you agree that possibly you didn't see that video until some two or three years or more after your release?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I must have seen a different one. This was not the one. They were seated in a room, drinking and singing. I believe there was a woman or a man who were having their leg amputated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question is really when you saw this video. Could it be that you didn't see the video until after 1995? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I do know that it was awhile after my exchange, but I can't give you the exact point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And then finally, you said that you recognised Naser Oric when you saw this trial broadcast on TV. I take it that was the initial appearance in April 2003. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On that occasion he was clean-shaven again. When you saw him on TV.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this is more than ten years after you say you saw Naser Oric at the prison on three brief occasions, when I think you said your brain was practically numb, you couldn't remember anything, and you couldn't even think straight. Is it right when you saw the broadcast you saw Mr. Oric standing between two UN guards and being addressed as Naser Oric and responding, "Yes, I'm Naser Oric"? Is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't need to check. I realised immediately that it was Mr. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you had been contacted at that point as a witness in the case against Mr. Oric, hadn't you, because you'd given a statement in 2000.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You had never been asked to pick Mr. Oric out of an identity parade, had you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've never been asked to identify Naser Oric from a selection of photographs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, I think the ELMO as it is now will stand in the way between Mr. Jones and the witness. Could you either push it forward or backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that the first time you mentioned to anyone that you had recognised Naser Oric on these two occasions was when you told us that last Friday when you came to court?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Before you gave testimony here, you were interviewed or you spoke to members of the Office of the Prosecutor. You didn't tell them, did you, that you had recognised Naser Oric on two -- on a video and when he testified here?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I note for the record that the proofing notes we received in relation to this witness didn't mention that, and it's such an important matter that I'm sure the Prosecution wouldn't deliberately omit that from the proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you don't know for a fact, do you, whether Veselin Sarac knew Naser Oric from before the war, do you? You thought perhaps he did because Sarac had an apartment in Srebrenica, but he never specifically told you that he knew Oric from before the war.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from Sarac. I know that for certain. You may have noticed the other day I denied parts of the statement that he made. Sarac said that he had known Mr. Naser before the war and he owns a flat in Srebrenica. He still does. His daughter lives in it. Unfortunately, Sarac has deceased but his daughter remains in that flat in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But Sarac didn't necessarily know everyone in Srebrenica municipality before the war, did he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't know every single man, can you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Doesn't that also assume that Naser Oric is from Srebrenica town, as opposed to from some other location within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. What Veselin Sarac told me is that he had known Mr. Naser before the war, and that's what I'm telling you now. As for the accuracy of that bit of information, I don't know. It should be easy enough for you to verify that, but that was what I heard. Now, where he hails from, whether he's from Srebrenica or elsewhere, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, last Thursday you told us that during your stay in prison, which would have been more than 20 days, I take it, you saw the person calling himself Naser Oric three times. I think the "da" wasn't interpreted, but it doesn't matter. Three times only.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about those visits, and I can take it shortly. You told us the first time was several days after your capture, so I take it that's in late September 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The second time is when this person brought meat, and I don't think you told us when that was, but would that still be in late September?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was late September or early October. I don't know the exact date, but it was soon after the first introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To try and fix it in time, you mentioned that a postman from Fakovici arrived ten days after you. Would it have been before he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrived?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before he arrived that this -- the meeting where the person brought --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the postman arrived, which would mean that it was sometime in October that Mr. Naser brought meat to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you didn't tell this postman, "Someone called Naser visited us and brought us meat"? That's not something you told him, because it happened when he was there.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I mean is when the postman arrived, you didn't say to him, "There's someone called Naser who has been coming and bringing us meat," did you, because that happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I be telling the postman if he was there himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That was all. Now, just sticking with this second visit, the person who brought you meat was nice towards you, wasn't he; he offered you meat?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And he thought that you didn't want to eat because the meat might be poisoned, so he ate it to show you that it was okay?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So he didn't notice that it was the problems with your teeth which stopped you from eating the meat?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told Mr. Naser Oric that my teeth hurt and that I couldn't eat meat. He asked me what had happened. I said I had caught a cold because of the opening in the wall, some sort of a window, did not have a glass pane, but I did not have the courage to say what exactly had happened to my teeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You weren't afraid of this person who was offering you meat, were you, at that stage? You were frightened that the guards would learn if you spoke of what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why would I be afraid of someone like that who came and brought meat? I would not have had any reason to be afraid of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to the third time that you say you saw Naser, that wasn't in your cell but it was in another room just before your exchange.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right, then, that while the postman from Fakovici was in your cell from the 5th to the 16th of October, 1992, that this person calling himself Naser came to your cell once, when he brought meat?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember he came to the cell twice, and the third time I saw him was on the 25th of October, 1992, so just before the exchange. I can't remember any other time he came. He might have, it's just that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you didn't leave your cell much during the whole time that you were in the prison, did you? You told us that you even avoided going to the toilet. So is it right that during the day you were in the prison pretty much -- you were in the cell pretty much the whole time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during the day, it was pretty quiet as well, wasn't it, with the five of you sitting there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So any conversations which took place with guards or other people visiting the cell would be something which would be overheard by all of you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to leave this area and go to a completely different area now, and that's to ask you some questions about your arrest on the 24th of September. So apologies if I appear to be skipping around, but I'm sure you can follow. Now, going back to the day of your arrest, you told us you were arrested at Bracan, which is an elevation above the bauxite mine. Now the mine itself was at Gunjaci, wasn't it? The actual mine was at Gunjaci or Gunjace?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's Gunjace, near Bracan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might just be helpful for all of us to have on the monitor a map of these places. So if I can ask for the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me take -- in fact, I left my glasses at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, not to worry. Perhaps I can just, for the benefit of the Court, indicate some places on the map. Then by describing their location, perhaps Mr. Radic will agree with the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We need to work on the contrast a little bit. Is it possible to change the colour so it's more green? The letters don't appear very clearly there. No. Okay. Not to worry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I might state so, that the fact that the witness won't be able to see the map or assist in the places on the map actually leads to the situation where we have Defence counsel testifying. We would suggest instead of that, we have a very rudimentary loop if we would like to be able to have the witness possibly use this, that might assist Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. I think at the same time I think basically I can direct the technicians to focus on Gunjace, which is the area shaded at the bottom -- yes, exactly, so that we enlarge --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if we could pull back, please. Thank you, Your Honour. I certainly have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time I think this should help the witness see better, and then of course I appreciate your offer, Ms. Sellers. The usher can hand him the magnifying glass or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, we need your help, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly didn't intend to give evidence. What I was going to do is by describing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Don't waste your time on that, Mr. Jones. For these matters, there's always a simple solution. So -- can -- Mr. Radic, I would -- I suggest that you look at your monitor rather than at the map. Look at the monitor, because there you can see better. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then if you need to look at the map, then use the magnifying glass that you have been given. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic. It was just to see firstly if you can locate Gunjace on that map and then Bracan near it. Do you see that? If not, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very well without my glasses, but I can see, if you want me to show on the screen, Bracan is here. It's written. That's where I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm only going to ask you one more question about that map. When you were arrested, you recognised some people from Djile, didn't you, for example, Sifet and Rifet Malovic. Firstly, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Djile is on the road just around the corner, it appears, from the mine. Djile is near the mine. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, maybe a kilometre and a half or two away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'll leave that for the moment. You also saw Mirzet Malovic on the day of your arrest, who was a driver whom you knew from the mine. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mirzet, Rifet and Sifet and are brothers who used to work with me together at the mine, and I recognised them straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You recognised Sifet and Rifet. Did you also see Mirzet on the day of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirzet I saw. I believe he was the bus driver. But I saw him at Viogor, at the house of Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when he saw you, did he hit you on the head with a knife handle?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Thursday in relation to Zulfo -- and I'll quote from the transcript. It's page 15, lines 16 to 17: "A relative of mine had been in prison together with Zulfo before the war. It was most likely that it was he who saved me then." And that is saved you from further mistreatment. Now when you said "he," were you referring to Zulfo saving you from further mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was saved by my cousin, because they had been in prison together before the war. My cousin's name is also Radic, and he asked me what this Radic was to me, and I said it was my cousin. And I believe it helped a lot later. They didn't beat me so much. And three of their guards went to that house in Viogor, awaiting further orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But your cousin is a Serb, I take it. You're not saying he was present on the 24th of September when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean, the cousin?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The cousin who was in prison with Zulfo. He wasn't there on that day.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when you say he saved you, don't you mean mentioning his name to Zulfo saved you from further mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you understood me, but I believe it was my cousin who saved me, because when Zulfo asked me what this Nedjelko Radic [as interpreted] was to me, I said it was my cousin, and from that moment on they didn't maltreat me or beat me any more. On the other hand, he ordered those three guards who had escorted me to go to -- back to that house and await further orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to clarify one matter, is your cousin's name also Nedjelko Radic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am Nedjelko Radic and my cousin is Milenko [Realtime transcript read in error "Rakingo"].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're the only Nedjelko Radic in Milici, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right that Zulfo didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I see that on line 17 -- page 17 line 1 it says, according to the transcript, "No, I am Nedjelko Radic and my cousin is Rakingo." He said Milenko, not Rakingo, just for the record. Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. Jones, but I think better correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right that Zulfo personally didn't physically mistreat you in any way? He didn't kick you or hit you or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Zulfo himself who captured me, and he was the first one to hit me. He held a kitchen knife in his hand, this big perhaps. Maybe 20 centimetres long, together with the handle. And with that knife, as far as I learned later, he slit the throat of Rajko Pantic, an employee of the mine who worked as a security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can stop there, stop you there. That opens a whole host of questions which I'm not going to go into because that wasn't mentioned in your examination-in-chief, and I don't think you've ever mentioned that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not relevant either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us that when you were arrested, you were a civilian mine worker. So you weren't in the RS army, then, the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no army of Republika Srpska there at the time. As for Milici, Vlasinci, Bratunac, Srebrenica, the army was never active there, not before the war, not during the war. And there was no military installation in this region before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also told us on Thursday that you didn't have a gun with you that day and didn't shoot, and I'm going to read exactly what you said on Thursday and then move on to what you told us on Friday, and I apologise if it's lengthy but I need to go through it. Now, on Thursday, and it's pages 15 to 16 of the transcript, lines 18 to 25, you said: "There were those two rifles, and I don't know if you gentlemen and ladies are aware of it. Those are M-48 rifles which can take five rounds plus one in the barrel. Two rifles of that kind remained with Slavko and Krnja at that house because they had carried the rifles in the first place. Of course they returned gunfire and ran out of ammunition, and we didn't need the empty rifles any more because we were going to Bracan and our rifles were up there in Bracan in a small cottage normally used for camping, where we spent our nights. And we never reached them, i.e., never reached our rifles, because of what happened. Zoran and Vidoje were killed and I was captured, without any weapon, that is." Now, that's what you told us on Thursday. My question is, firstly, that gives the impression, what you told us, doesn't it, that Slavko and Krnja were shooting and ran out of ammunition, not you. That's the impression you gave last Thursday. I will move on. Then last Friday we saw the video in which you said you were captured in combat and that you ran out of ammunition, and when you were asked about that in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour I hate to interrupt counsel, but I think that he did state here, "Now my question is first that that gives the impression ..." and then he continues on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But I don't believe he was given the opportunity to answer the question. I just want to know is counsel actually narrating something or has he asked a question he would like the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm coming to a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's coming to a question, and I think it's an obvious question that he's going to put, so go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were asked about this in cross-examination after we saw the video, and it's page 16, line 17 to 19, you said: "I believe that since I was shooting at them and they were shooting at me, it was combat. Of course, I ran out of ammunition, then I dropped my gun." Now, my question is this: Was it when you saw the video and heard yourself saying that you ran out of ammunition that you realised that you had to change your story and admit that you had been shooting, whereas before you sought to suggest that Slavko and Krnja were doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that Slavko and Krnja did any shooting. As far as I remember my talks with the Prosecution, I said I was carrying a rifle. I didn't say Krnja or Slavko had a weapon. After the shooting started from Bijelo Polje, from Kutuzari village directed at us, I returned fire, and that's what I remember saying in my statement to the Prosecution. I said exactly how many rounds I had, five plus one in the barrel, that's the maximum the rifle will take. And after shooting all of the rounds, I threw the rifle to Slavko. Krnja had another rifle. Some of them stayed in that house, and the two of us went back to Bracan. And since there was an exchange of fire, I thought it qualified as combat. Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Radic, but you didn't make that clear to this Court when you testified on Thursday, that you were shooting and returning fire. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is making it clear now, Mr. Jones, and it's -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. But it's a question of how truthful this witness is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why I make the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On the 24th of September, 1992, didn't you also throw a grenade or a bomb at the attackers?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Something else you didn't mention, isn't it? You threw a bomb or a grenade at the attacking forces.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where would I get a grenade? A grenade is something that you don't launch with your own hand. You need something to launch it with. There is a special section shooting grenades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because again this is how, then, the wrong interpretation can be given to the text or the transcript. The question, as I read it on -- in line 17 was: "On the 24th of September, 1992, didn't you also throw a grenade or a bomb at the attackers?" And according to the transcript, the witness said, "Yes," which would mean that he did. But if you continue reading, it's obvious that he never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thought he said "da," but in fact he may have said "ja."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. So I'm going to call on you again, Mr. Radic, because when we read the transcript it's as if, to that question, you admitted having thrown a grenade or a bomb at the attackers. Did you at any time on the 24th of September, 1992, throw any grenade or any bomb or even a hand grenade on the attackers or at the attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, how would I throw a hand grenade or any other grenade when the attackers who were shooting at us were two or three kilometres away? It's impossible without a special weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not arguing with you, Mr. Radic, I just wanted an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I take it the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, do you recall being interviewed about these events in 1994, in August, the 25th of August, to be precise? Not by this Tribunal but by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have copies of the 1994 statement which, if the witness could be shown the B/C/S version, and there are copies for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, before you proceed, Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to make sure. Did you ask whether he was

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: authorities of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: By the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: By the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the statement of the 18th November 1999, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. It's 25th of August, 1994. ERN is 03602052 to 03602059.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'd ask you to first of all look at the foot of each page and to look at the signature at the bottom. Use the magnifying glass if you like, because I'd like you to take a very good look at the signature. Can you please have a look at that signature and tell us whether you recognise that as your signature or not.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And can we turn through each page just to make sure, absolutely sure. Is that your signature on every page?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's an eight-page statement, so I'm not going to ask you to read through the whole statement, but I am going to refer you to certain passages. And in English I'll start with page 3. And the ERNs are the same for the English and B/C/S. So it's 03602054. It's page 3 of both versions, paragraphs 1 and 2. And there we see the words: "Among the Muslim soldiers who came there, apart from Zulfo Tursunovic, I also recognised Malovic Sifet from the village of Djile, his brother Rifet." So those are the brothers you mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And the next paragraph you mention some of the killed Serbs you saw, Salipurevic, Slavko, Boris Music, which I think should be Miso Misic, perhaps. If you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I was probably mistaken about the last name. It could be Boric from the Misic village, from Milici.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And Rajko Pantic, a worker from the Miletici mine. Those were the people you saw. And then on the next page, on page 4, first paragraph, you refer to Mirzet Malovic and the story you told us just now, about seeing him in Viogor. Now, my question is: Seeing your signature, seeing those details, do you accept that this statement records what you told the person interviewing you in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Is this the statement which you gave in August 1994? Do you recognise it as such?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what you read so far, yes, it seems to be, but I didn't throw any grenades.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'll ask this -- I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask this to be given a Defence exhibit number, the 1994 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be -- this document is being admitted as Defence Exhibit, being marked as D156.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, you can keep the statement with you because I'm going to ask you about it. Let's turn back to the beginning of that statement. You told us today that you were a civilian mine worker. Now, looking at that statement, the first three paragraphs on page 2, ERN 03602053, I quote, "As the RS army soldier under the command in Milici on September 24 -- sorry, September 23, 1992, I was assigned to secure the bauxite mine in Milici, the area called Bracan. This place, which was secured by my squad, was suddenly attacked by Muslim armed forces on September 24, 1992, at about 9.30 a.m. At that moment I was going to get some water with soldiers Salipurevic Vidoje, Lalovic Zoran from Milici, and Gordic Slavko and Susic Milivoje, also from Milici. When we were halfway to the water spring, shooting suddenly started and we went back to our positions, not knowing what it was all about." See here you described yourself, didn't you, and others, as RS soldiers, whereas now you say you were a civilian; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear gentlemen, you are not right, because unfortunately I couldn't be a soldier. I didn't qualify to be a soldier, and I said so in my statement. However, every municipality in the former Yugoslavia had its Territorial Defence. This Territorial Defence had its weaponry, had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. I'm just reading what's in this statement, and it refers to RS army, not to Territorial Defence. That's what I was seeking to establish. I'm going to come back to that in a moment. I just want to continue to the next paragraph. "As our tank was nearby, as well as a group of uniformed soldiers, I thought that they were our soldiers and hurried towards my position to see why they were shooting. I climbed on a boundary. My dugout was behind it. They started shooting from the immediate vicinity, and I lay down and threw a bomb in the direction from which they fired at me." I don't know if you can see that. I think you're not actually reading your statement, but that's the -- that's what's in the English. Now, I have a number of questions for you arising from these passages. Firstly, this is a very different account, isn't it, from the one that you've given us here. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again that I was not a soldier, because everybody knows perfectly well what an army is. I served in the army in 1970. You know the distinction between a soldier, a civilian, a worker.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. But my question is this account is very different from the one which you gave us before this Court. That was my question. I'm not asking you to go into this distinction again between the Territorial Defence and the RS. Now, let's go through it. You've told us here, under oath, that you were a mere civilian, guarding the mine with an M-48 with other civilians. And in this statement you describe the situation of an RS soldier in an squad with an assigned task, taking positions, having a tank, and throwing bombs at the enemy. Now, are you saying you didn't say those things?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this, that's one thing. Secondly, we never had a tank. There was a unit in Vlasenica, some sort of an armoured combat unit, young lads up to 25 years of age, single. They were some sort of Intervention Platoon, the one that they set up at municipality level in the event of an attack. They had two APCs, and as for ourselves we had nothing except for our mining equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: There was a tank, a T53, up at Bracan on the day of your arrest, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was later after my arrest, but I don't remember that there were any around before.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Well, you know Bracan very well, I take it, at this time. You were guarding the area day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Either there was a tank there and you would have seen it, or there wasn't. You're not telling us that there might have been a tank up where you were guarding and you didn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see a tank. Again, I must say maybe it was after I had been captured that a tank arrived or that a unit arrived to help out. But when I was there, I don't remember seeing any tank.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: How about heavy artillery, anti-aircraft guns and that sort of thing? Surely if that was on Bracan you would have noticed that because that's fixed.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only a three-barrelled weapon at Bracan and a 180-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And that three-barrelled gun and the mortar were firing at Muslim villages like Suceska, weren't they, shooting at Muslim towns and villages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have a new exhibit, document for everyone. It's a document of the Srebrenica War Presidency, dated 25 September 1992, and the ERN is 01801622, 01801623. It describes the events of 24th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would just like to state for the record that the Prosecution did receive a list of these exhibits yesterday evening but did not have the benefit of these exhibits prior to the witness having direct examination conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We found them over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need to make a correction. The exhibit number for the previous exhibit has to be D158 and not D156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So please, Prosecution and Defence, do enter a correction in your records. The statement in B/C/S starting with ERN 03602052 up to and inclusive of 03602059, and the corresponding English translation of the same, bearing the same ERN number, are being marked as Defence Exhibit D158 and not as D156 as previously inadvertently or mistakenly indicated. So this one now will become D159.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So don't make any further mistakes. And of course I have -- we have taken into consideration your remark, Ms. Sellers, which is perfectly logical. I mean, it's -- obviously, you will have an opportunity to re-examine the witness later on. Take into consideration what you have said. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before we turn to the new exhibit, may I just come back to D158. I just realised that the statement given by the witness, according to this document, was on the 25th of August of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And there is a signature down there was of 19 August of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's another signature altogether. That's a signature of the Judge, Vaso Eric, when he was shown this document. The signature we're concerned with is the one to the right of that, which doesn't bear that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could the accused be asked whether his signature was put on this when he was examined in 1994 or whether it was on the occasion of the 19th of August 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 19/08/2004 is an altogether different signature, so I don't think it would be appropriate to put that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I do understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we want to know is -- Mr. Radic, you were shown before this statement that supposedly you made to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska in way back on the 25th of August, 1994, and you were shown your signatures on different pages, and you accepted that this was your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did you sign these documents; in 1994 when you were interviewed, or later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't remember whether it was before or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But when you were interviewed in 1994 by the officer of Republika Srpska, by one of the investigative judges, and you were being asked questions and you were answering questions, what was the procedure? Was it being typed out or was it being recorded? And if it was recorded, when were you given the text to sign; on that same day or later? And if later, how much later? Let's take them one by one. On the 25th of August, 1994, you were interviewed by an officer of Republika Srpska. Here we have an indication that it was a certain Trajkovic Gorica. Trajkovic Gorica. You may or may not remember. Where did the interview take place; in Zvornik or in your own residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't remember. I can't remember the year or the place of the interview. What I do know is that I was interviewed, but I can't remember the year or the place of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you remember whether you signed the document on that same day you were interviewed or not or later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. This is my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. signature, but I can't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can leave it at that, safely leave it at that because it's not going to change anything, but the point is made that Judge Vaso Eric's signature comes later when obviously --

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: So looking at D159, the document of the Srebrenica War Presidency, I'm going to read from part of that and ask you some questions. We see on the first page: "Around 1000 hours on 24 September 1992, Serbian Chetnik criminals from Podravanje and Milici attacked the villages of Kutuzari, Lipovac, and Suceska, using the most destructive hardware that the Yugoslav soldiery had given them. There were casualties among the innocent civilian population. The most notorious criminals from Podravanje and Derventa were unsuccessfully trying to move the front line. In a speedy and effective action, the Srebrenica armed forces moved to counter-attack on the line between Zutica, Suceska, Kutuzari and Bucje villages. In an exceptionally well prepared sabotage action the Chetnik Bracan stronghold was taken, a T-53 tank and a PAT anti-aircraft gun were quickly seized from the aggressor and two armoured personnel carriers were destroyed. A great deal of artillery and infantry ammunition, grenades and other MTS (material and technical equipment) was seized in the action." Then in the fourth paragraph on the next page, the document states how the Serbs then launched hundreds of shells at Srebrenica in retaliation, wounding many civilians, and the Yugoslav air force carried out raids, wounding and killing dozens of people. My question is: Isn't that the reality as described in that document, and given that you were there and you know what was going on, that's something you saw with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't say that Bracan was the only place where weapons were stationed. There was Podravanje, there was Gunjace. I'm not a military expert myself to know exactly where weapons were positioned. I was at Bracan so I know what was there but I know nothing about the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Exactly. So you know, don't you, that Bracan was a stronghold with heavy artillery and anti-aircraft gun and that they were firing from there onto Muslim villages. I put it to you that's something you know to be the case.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one mortar and one three-barrelled gun there, speaking of artillery. There was nothing else. There were seven or eight of us guards who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- so basically what has been read out to you by Mr. Jones, particularly this second paragraph of this document, you don't agree with? Am I right? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that has just been read back to me, no, I disagree with the part about the weapons. I don't agree that those weapons were there. The tanks were in Vlasenica with the units. I believe it was referred to as an assault platoon or something of the kind. At the mine it would have been impossible. I don't know about the nearby woods, but I didn't go there. This is more or less all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: This was a pretty heavily militarised area, though, wasn't it? We've seen in your 1994 statement reference to your positions and a dugout. Isn't it the case that this was actually heavily fortified front lines against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we need to clarify one thing. A trench is one thing, and bunkers are a different thing. There were no bunkers there. There were trenches that were dug in a very primitive way, so you could just dig down and the enemy couldn't see you. But there were no bunkers. There were just two or three shallow trenches around Bracan. There was a trailer where we slept, and that was all we had.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And isn't it also right, didn't Sarac even admit when interviewed, when he said of the events of the 24th of September, 1992, in Podravanje that, I'm quoting from the transcript: "They, the attackers, captured a lot of weapons from us, light and heavy." Isn't that correct, a lot of light and heavy weapons were captured from the Serbs that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'm telling you Sarac was captured in Podravanje. I told you that I'd never gone to Podravanje. The distance between Bracan and Podravanje is three or four kilometres. I had no need to go there and I have no idea what was happening there. Sarac must have known, but his statement is not true. It's his statement, but I really can't tell you what was going on over there because we were captured at two different places.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Sarac said a lot of things when interviewed which weren't true, didn't he? You mentioned two yesterday, and that seems to be a third one which you're saying he said but which was not true.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that it's true or that it's not true. I simply wasn't there and I don't know. It's possible that his statement is true. I just can't confirm or deny it because I simply wasn't present. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, the document we just saw also refers to mercenaries from Serbia, referring to Chetniks who were killed and mercenaries from Serbia. The guard which you were in included people from Serbia, didn't it? Kukic and Nevenko were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not with me there. They were in a different place. They were hired by the bauxite mine as some sort of help. You should be able to check that with the company itself, but I have no idea who brought them over or who paid them.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: But they weren't there to work as miners, were they? They didn't work in the mine. They were purely acting as guards.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I really would like to make sure that counsel's characterisation of volunteer guards differs from what I recall Mr. Radic stating that these were employees. No one has brought forward a notion of volunteer employees and I would like to know if that's what counsel is trying to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Point -- point taken, and I think, however, if one reads the transcript, that emerges quite clear, because although it's true that Mr. Jones did hint these may have been volunteer guards, the witness's reply is very clear that they were hired by the company as guards, which excludes what was -- what was suggested to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. My suggestion is that Nevenko and Kukic could be described as mercenaries from Serbia because they're being paid to fight in a war in a country which was not theirs. That's what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree with what Mr. Jones has just stated now, Mr. Radic? It's being put to you that respective of what you have just said yourself, these two gentlemen can be described as mercenaries from Serbia because they were paid to fight in a war in a country which was not theirs. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. They were not paid to fight. They were hired by the company on a three-month contract to watch the mine, to provide security. Secondly, these two persons, Kukic was over 60 years of age at the time. I don't think he would have been fit enough to take part in combat, a man aged over 60. What can he possibly do?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Moving to another area, and it's a short topic, so I think I can deal with it before the break. You told us on Thursday that the bauxite mine was the second largest bauxite mine in Europe. It was worth a lot, wasn't it, the mine, to whichever side controlled it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And in September 1992, the Serbs controlled it, controlled the mine, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As well as earlier. Prior to 1992, I mean. Prior to September 1992, because the mine itself was never taken. It was Serb controlled throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: It was controlled from May or June 1992 when all the Muslims left the mine. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, you've accepted that the mine was the primary source of raw materials to produce aluminium. Among others, it supplied the Birac-Zvornik aluminium factory in Zvornik, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That factory was also controlled by the Serbs from early in the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Weren't both the aluminum mine and the bauxite mine very important for the Serb war effort, for financing the war effort?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the clay factory or the mine did not operate throughout the war. Maybe earlier. Maybe up until November, but later there were stops, and it was operating below capacity. One day there would be five lorries taking the ore away and the next day two. There was not enough food for locals to go around let alone petrol for the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Wasn't the bauxite mine, firstly, a fiefdom in a sense of Rade Bjelanovic who was very involved both in ethnic cleansing and prosecuting the war on behalf of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Rade Bjelanovic was police chief in Milici when the war broke out. I have no idea what they did. There is no way for me to know. I think you should ask Rade Bjelanovic himself. One thing you must know is that an ordinary citizen can't be familiar with what's going on in -- within the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: He was the manager of the bauxite mine as well, wasn't he, Rade Bjelanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in a leading position, but he was not the director, the manager, himself.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the Muslims, 1.500 Muslims approximately, left the mine in May 1992. Now, at this time jobs were scarce, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I think about 3.000 Muslims. My rough estimate was 50/50. That means there must have been around 1.500 Muslims. This is not necessarily accurate, but it was thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: My point is a different one, which is that at this time, with the war starting and all those problems, jobs outside the mine, leaving the mine for one moment, they weren't very available, were they, so that people wouldn't just leave their jobs and their livelihood just for the hell of it. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no pressure for them to leave their jobs. That's one thing I know for certain. I believe I said this in one of my statements. It was on a Thursday. The parties, the ICS and the SDA, divided people, and obviously once this division was introduced the Serbs followed their leaders and the Muslims followed theirs. So this was the underlying reason for people leaving their jobs.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's precisely my point, though, Mr. Radic; that you're linking people leaving their jobs, their source of livelihood, when other jobs are not easily available, and you're suggesting that somehow that's linked to the formation of the SDA. And so my question is why would people leave well-paid jobs, which you told us was a source of pride to work at the mine, unless they were forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, they were not forced to leave. The war began. What I believe is when you have a war going on, you hardly have any -- I'm not sure how I should put this. Privileges. You can't choose if you want war or not. You may leave any day. But I'm sure this was due to the war breaking out, the whole thing. And probably people much like myself felt unsafe staying there with the war on. If I had been a Muslim, I would have felt very much the same.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's what I'm --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were the predominant group.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Yes. If I could stop you there because you're giving fairly lengthy answers and I need to keep your answers short if we are to finish today. That's precisely what I'm getting at. Why would the Muslims at the mine feel unsafe staying at the mine when the Serbs felt perfectly happy staying there and working there? Why did the Muslims feel unsafe?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's difficult for me to explain. I think you should ask someone else. I have no idea why. I can only talk about my own personal case, but I can't provide any answers in relation to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I think you're being evasive, Mr. Radic. Isn't it obvious that -- and wasn't it obvious to you at the time, that the Muslims left their jobs, 1.500 of them, because they were intimidated and frightened and bullied so that they would leave the mine because the Serbs were taking it over?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea who bullied them or who pushed them to leave. I don't know. If I knew, I'd be certain to tell you who it was that did it or why. But honestly, I don't know, and that's why I simply can't answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: One more question before the break. I'm not asking you who, I'm just asking if you confirm that that's what happened, that they were bullied by someone to leave the mine.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what camp you're talking about. Mine, oh, okay. I don't know about that. All I can is I don't know who made them or whether anyone did, for that matter. There were Muslims working there. They stayed on until sometime in October, those who worked in the mine. Therefore, not all of them left immediately. It took place in stages, in a manner of speaking, but they continued to work there, and there are people who worked there who have in the meantime returned, the same people who used to work there before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. We will have a 25-minute break. How much longer do you have so that we give the Prosecution an indication of when to prepare the other witness, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm making quite good progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'll probably be finished by the next break, although there is the possibility that I will go slightly after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But we could certainly start with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We will have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, before the break, you were telling us how Muslims left the Bracan mine in stages. My question is: Don't those stages correspond to the stages of ethnic cleansing of Muslims from their villages in the Vlasenica area? That is, Muslims stopped coming to the mine after they had been chased from their villages.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure that they were chased out. It's not within my competence, and I know nothing about it. I told you a moment ago that I was a regular citizen just like anyone else. You should ask somebody from a higher level whether they were expelled or not.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm asking you, and the questions I put to you I'd be grateful if you would answer if you can and otherwise not. There's no need to suggest that I should speak to anyone else, if you understand. And it would also -- it would also be helpful to make progress if you keep your answers short.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's okay. Now, you told us that you wouldn't know anything about ethnic cleansing of Muslim villages, but you're from Milici, you work -- you worked, at the time, in Bracan, and there's a road which goes from Milici down to Bracan which passes lots of Muslim villages on the road, Pomol, Besici, Nurici, Stedra, Djile. Now, what I'm saying is you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. passed those villages, you saw them, and surely you would be aware if the houses had been burnt and the inhabitants had been expelled. So are you saying it didn't happen, or are you saying that you didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there's too much in one question. Perhaps you could break it -- break it down in various stages, Mr. Jones, because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know exactly what I mean. It's loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You're familiar, Mr. Radic, with the Muslim villages of, and I'll do them one by one, Pomol. Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pomol.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: So you're familiar with that Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And it's on or near the road between Milici and the mine where you worked?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not close to the main road but maybe two or three kilometres away from the road.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: How about Besici, also a Muslim village, also one which is not far from the main road?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Nurici is really right on the road, isn't it, and a Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And the same for Stedra as well? It's actually on the road and it was a Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that on September 24, 1992, just to take a date, that the Muslims were all living in all those villages at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You maintain that Muslims were living without any harassment, in September 1992, in, for example, Nurici. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not there in September. I believe sometime in May, not later than June, they left their villages. Naturally, because most of these people that lived in those villages worked in the bauxite mine.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm getting at. Muslims leaving their villages in May/June 1992, that's what I'm asking you about, that's a pretty significant event, isn't it, Muslims leaving their villages? That's something which you confirm occurred.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know the reason why.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Is that your honest answer, you don't know why they left, or do you know that they left because they were brutally, brutally expelled, ethnically cleansed by Serb forces from their villages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My honest opinion, to the best of my knowledge, as I said, those people worked at the bauxite mine, and when they left the bauxite company, it was natural for them to go elsewhere. Where, I don't know. And they took their families with them, as I would take my family if I was moving. And to be honest, of course there were attacks on those villages just as Muslim forces attacked Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's it. I'm asking you to be honest and to tell us frankly about attacks on their villages and not to hold back. And that's what I've been trying to get you to help us with. Isn't it true that Muslims left their villages because they were attacked and their houses were burnt?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, as I said a moment ago, those villages were attacked, but I don't know about it. I didn't participate in those attacks. I cannot tell you about things that I don't know anything about, but there were attacks on those villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And the people who left didn't just go elsewhere, as you said, they went and lived in the woods across on the other side of the road, didn't they, because they had nowhere else to go?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't go to the woods. You didn't mention a place called Zutica. I didn't see it on the map. It's between Besici hill and the village of -- let me think for a moment. I can't remember the name of the village, but if you go from Milici it's on the left. Zutica I couldn't find on the map. There was a passage from there towards the mine only after Srebrenica fell, which means that those Muslims from the surrounding villages were there. Zutica, Zabensko [phoen], and others towards Srebrenica. So they didn't go to the woods, they were there, close by.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Did you also hear in relation to attacks on villages that there was a massacre in Zaklopaca in which women and children were killed, and also killings in Pomol, as well as in Nurici and the other places that I mentioned? Did you hear about that or any of those events?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Zaklopaca, that there was indeed a massacre there, and I can confirm that with certainty. As for the other places, they were attacked. Whether any other massacres were involved, I don't know, but if there were attacks, of course there were casualties and people killed, wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And that's the massacre of Muslims in Zaklopaca, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Are you aware of Susica camp in Vlasenica where Muslims were held, where Dragan Jenki Nikolic, convicted by this Tribunal of crimes against humanity, was a camp commander? Did you know about Susica?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never went near that camp. I didn't need to go there. It's in the Vlasenica municipality. Milici was then part of the Vlasenica municipality, as a matter of fact, but I heard about the existence of that camp, and I also heard that things happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Let's deal with Milici, then, because you're from there and obviously you knew Milici well at the time. Wasn't there a huge military presence in Milici in September 1992 with armoured transport units, tanks, transporters, artillery, and even units which had fought in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. I know that, as required, those armoured units came from Vlasenica. But I know that we had no tanks or APCs. They were located in Vlasenica, and they would come as required. Milici was, at the time, under the Vlasenica municipality, and now it's separate.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: There was a Milici Brigade, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in October, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I'd like to show the witness a new document, new exhibit. It's from the SJB public security station Milici, dated 28 May 1992. And the ERN is 01782455, and it's a duty report of the police station in Milici. I want to draw your attention and the witness's attention to the section under "Vehicles," where it states that: "All vehicles were used to cleanse the field in the area of Milici Brdo." And at the bottom under the note, that: "Two police squads led by R. Bjelanovic and R. Pantic were cleansing the areas in Koprivno and providing support to the local population."

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And my question to you, Mr. Radic, is wasn't there ethnic cleansing of Muslims from the Koprivno area in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Koprivno is a Serb area with a 100 Serb population.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Let's take that one stage at a time. Firstly, dealing with R. Bjelanovic, there, would you agree that that most probably refers to Rade Bjelanovic, the manager of the bauxite mine and the person whose voice you identified on the audiotape?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
