utterances.text: Yes, it is Rade Bjelanovic. But Rade Bjelanovic was never director of the bauxite company. He was an administrator of one of the units, and he was my boss, my manager, and he's the same Rade whom we heard on the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And the R. Pantic in that document, could that be the R. Pantic from the mine who was killed on the 24th of September, if you know? Did he work with Rade Bjelanovic in cleansing operations?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, which question does Defence counsel want the witness to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Really, it's an attempt to clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a case of rephrasing it, Mr. Jones, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: In the document I've just referred to there's a note which reads as follows: "Two police squads that were cleansing the areas in Koprivno and provided support to population in this area led by the head Bjelanovic, R., and the commander Pantic, R., returned to Milici at 6.30 p.m." My question would be R. Pantic referred to in that document, could that be the Pantic from the mine who died on the 24th of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, sir - I'm sorry, I don't know your name - the place of Koprivno is a Serb place with 100 per cent Serb population, and Rajko Pantic, who was killed on the 24th of September, 1992, when I was captured at Bracan, is not the same Pantic. There is Radomir Pantic, sometimes called Rado, who was head of the Milici SUP, or the police.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Going back to Koprivno, there isn't any reason as to why Serb policemen would be conducting a cleansing operation in the sense of ethnically cleansing Serbs, is there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It must be a case of wrong information. I have already said, and I can confirm, that Koprivno is a Serb place.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: How about it referring possibly to cleansing the area in the sense of seeking out Muslims who had left their homes and hunting them down, killing them, capturing them? It could refer to that, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not going to allow the witness to answer this question because if you put the question to me, Mr. Jones, looking at this document, I would never even dare give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would simply ask that this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case, and then -- as we say in my own language, the Lord will try to understand. So this will be D160, and I think Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to have a question with regard to the term "cleansing." Now, in the Serbian Croatian language, does it have the same meaning or connotation as it is used in English? When we referring to cleansing, it's always meant in terms of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would prefer to leave the witness to answer that, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, how do you understand the term "cleansing" as used in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I did not participate in this. I never moved far from the mine. I would stand on guard eight days, rest for seven days, then work on the shop floor. So I moved between my home and the mine. I didn't go anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Two things: Firstly, that's not the question which we were asking; and secondly, you are tending to give quite lengthy answers, and I think we will want to finish with your testimony today. It's a question of language purely. Never mind whether you know of this action. In May 1992, if one said to you -- if a Serb policeman said to you, "We cleansed this area," what would you understand him to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course if he had said something like that to me, I would understand him to mean that it was cleansed of Muslim people, but nobody told me any such thing. And of course the police would not tell a civilian what they were doing, like the commander would not tell a regular soldier about his intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Could the interpreters who are interpreting from English into Bosnian Croat -- B/C/S, please tell me what word they use -- they used in translating Mr. Jones when he used the word "cleansed"? What word did you use in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's "ciscenje." I'm sorry, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want the interpreters to answer me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We use the term "ocistili."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is not "ciscenje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "A to nije," "ciscenje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let Mr. Radic -- look at me. If I used the words, "Koristana su sva vozila radi ciscenja terena na potezu Milica Brdo, Koprivno", what would you understand? When I use the word "ciscenje," what do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cleansing or cleaning, depends on the object. You can clean the road. You can cleanse a people. It depends on how it's used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Jones. I think we've got a clear answer. And thanks to the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm moving to an entirely different area now.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about your treatment in the prison. Firstly, I want to ask you about the very first night that you arrived at the SUP. And again, so we make progress, there's no need for you to retell your story at any stage. My questions will be specific. Now, firstly, in 1994 -- in your statement in 1994, speaking of the first night of your arrest, and I'm referring to page 4 of the English, the ERN is 03602055, fifth paragraph, "During the night they brought Veselin Sarac from Podravanje to the same room as well as Brankovic Zoran, about 18 years old from Smederevo, a volunteer of the RS army. They did not touch or maltreat us that night." And that's also what you told us last Thursday, and for the transcript it's page 27, lines 23 to 25, and page 28, line 1: "That first night that you were there, did anything happen to you in terms of physical mistreatment, the night that you arrived?" "No, no, not when we arrived." But if I could refer you now to your statement made in 2000 to ICTY investigators, a statement which you signed as truthful, and if we have that, it's page 5 of 12, ERN 02030468, and it's the 7th, last paragraph. You said: "During that first evening, after the two new prisoners came, the door to our cell opened, and two or three men came in and beat us. They hit us with their fists, and they kicked us all over our bodies. We were sitting on the floor, and they would kick and kick us. It was dark and no lights were on. I could not see them." Now, that's a clear statement, isn't it, about the first night that you were imprisoned, after the two other prisoners came in, and it completely contradicts what you told us last week and in your 1994 statement, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still stand by my statement to the effect that nobody even touched us that first evening. It could be a case of misinterpretation or a wrong date. It did happen that they entered our cell and beat us, but not on that first night.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I'm getting at, Mr. Radic. In your 2000 statement, it's a very clear statement, isn't it? It refers to the first evening after the two prisoners came in, and you say you were hit with fists, kicked all over your bodies, kicked and kicked. What I'm putting to you is there's no room for a mistake there. Whoever wrote that down was clearly under the impression that you told them that you were very badly beaten on your first evening, and in fact that's untrue. Are you saying that the ICTY investigator put that in your statement when it was not true?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not doubt the honesty of the Prosecution's investigators. I could have made an error and mixed things up and said this about the first evening, or maybe the interpreter didn't get it right.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You understand the need to give an accurate and truthful account of what happened to you in prison, and when you gave this statement you knew that it was for an investigation in the Oric case, and you signed it as being true to the best of your knowledge and belief after it was read Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. back to you, didn't you? What I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again there are a lot of questions in one question here. I mean, I very much doubt if he ever knew at the time about even the Oric case, and I don't know if it even existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: The point is this, Mr. Radic: Doesn't your account about what happened to you at the SUP change every time you tell this story?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which SUP you are talking about. The SUP in Srebrenica, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Of course. There's no other SUP which has been referred to. The SUP in Srebrenica. Let me put it a different way. I put it to you a moment ago that each time you speak about these events you give a different account. In one you're a civilian, in another you're an RS soldier in a squad. In one statement you're getting savagely beaten on your first night, in another statement you're left completely alone. So my question to you is: Are you what you're telling us -- is what you're telling us the fruit of genuine recollection, or are you making it up as you go along?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not making anything up. When you see something for yourself, you can't make it up. It's possible that I gave this statement about the first evening. I mean, it has been a long while, after all, and I would have been unable to remember every single thing. But I must say it again, the first evening no one touched us. The next evening they smashed my teeth and extracted them. I have no need in the world to make things up.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Sorry to have to insist on this, but another part of your story, what you told us, was obviously a very unpleasant memory of Kemo urinating in your mouth. And as I say, I'm sorry to have to ask you about it, but here in this Tribunal, when specifically asked about it, you said that Kemo urinated in your mouth. In your 2000 statement, you said that someone else altogether did it. I'm looking at page 9, ERN 02030472. "Kemo then ordered the soldier to pee in my mouth. Kemo said this will be good for you. Your wounds will be washed out. The soldier then peed in my mouth and the Kemo forced me to swallow it all." Then three paragraphs down, you refer to another instance, and you say: "This time Kemo said, 'This time there is no one who can wash your wounds out.'" Now, looking at this statement, whoever wrote this down was very clear, weren't they, that you told them that a soldier urinated in your mouth, not Kemo.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemo was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: But here you're saying that Kemo ordered another soldier to do that to you. And my point is this would be a vivid unpleasant memory, and I suggest it's impossible to get something like that wrong and that you've invented this part of the story.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't invent it. They urinated into my mouth. They extracted my teeth. Kemo, more specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'm referring you to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. So basically Mr. Jones has just put it to you that there are two versions to this unfortunate event. One version is what you said during your testimony here and what you seem to have repeated now, namely that it was Kemo who urinated in your mouth. The other version is what comes out, what emerges from the statement that was referred to, which does not state that Kemo urinated in your mouth but that Kemo ordered someone else, a soldier, to urinate in your mouth, and it was that soldier and not Kemo who urinated in your mouth. Which of the two versions is the correct one? Let's start from there.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemo. That is the true answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if that is so, what is your explanation for what is contained in the statement where it says that you were telling the investigators that it wasn't Kemo who urinated in your mouth but someone else who Kemo ordered to urinate in your mouth? How do you explain this difference? If you told the investigators "It was Kemo who urinated in my mouth," how on earth would the investigator write down that Kemo ordered someone else to urinate in your mouth? How do you explain the difference? This is what basically we want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I returned home in December, I had time to mull things over and to understand what was going on, and I realised that the same man named Kemo who had smashed my teeth, there was a table over there. He leaned my head against the table and then he urinated into my mouth. Therefore, it was Kemo. Kemo was the person. There was only Kemo around, after all. Mrki was there, too, and the turnkey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever tell anyone, any one of the investigators of the Office of the Prosecution, did you ever tell anyone that Kemo ordered a soldier to urinate in your mouth and that soldier urinated in your mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. He's all yours.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Let's look at your 1994 statement again, it's page 4, sixth paragraph. You don't need to look at it, I'll read it to you. This is now -- I want to ask you about the first interview at the SUP by the chief, Mirzet. So this is the next morning, 25th of September. I think you've been very clear that the first morning you were at the SUP, you were interviewed, and you say: "The next morning, between 10.00 and 11.00 a.m. they took us one by one for questioning to a room at the ground floor. They took me for questioning first. SUP chief Mirzet questioned me. They did not beat or maltreat me this time." And I think I'm right in saying that on the 1994 statement your signature is right by that line which says, "They did not beat or maltreat me this time." Now, let's look at what you said about exactly the same interview, the first questioning, the morning after you were brought in, in your 2000 statement. It's a bit lengthy but I'll read it out. It's page 6, ERN 02030469, second paragraph: "The next morning, I think around 9.00 a.m., but again I did not have my watch so I do not know the time for sure, that morning each of us was taken one by one to the chief's office for interrogation. A soldier who was dressed in a camouflage uniform took me to see the chief. Two other men were present. They were dressed in civilian clothes, as was the chief. None of them were carrying weapons. The chief explained that one man was a Croat and the other one was from the international community. The chief offered me a cigarette and lit it for me, then he began punching me and he told me that it would be my last cigarette. The chief kept asking me questions and hitting me. I was sitting in a chair and he slapped me, punched me, and he kicked me in the face with his foot. After the interrogation, I was taken back to the cell. I was bleeding from the mouth and nose." Now, that's, again I would put to you, a very specific reference to hitting, slapping, punching, kicking, and at the end that you were bleeding from the mouth and nose. Now, do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Yet on Friday you said something else again, and it's at page 30, line 16 to 20: "Now, when you went back to your cell --" this is referring to that same occasion -- "do you recall whether you were bleeding or not?" "No." Question: "No, you do not recall or no you were not bleeding?" "I was not bleeding." And that was on Thursday, and then you were very clear and categorical that you were not bleeding when you returned to your cell after your first interrogation on the 25th of September, 1992. Now, is that correct, that you weren't bleeding after the left the first interrogation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was not bleeding in the cell. It was in the office when the chief kicked me that my nose started bleeding, and my teeth too. Not much blood, though, just a little, and then it stopped. Back in the cell, I was no longer bleeding. There was this gentleman in civilian clothes, the chief, I think. The other two did not touch me.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: In your 1994 statement, you're saying that you weren't beaten or maltreated at all. Do you recall saying that when you were asked by the --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not those two, just the chief.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: These details may seem not so significant to you, Mr. Radic, whether you were beaten on the first night, whether you were bleeding or not after your interrogation, but I hope you appreciate we need to get this right. And it seems to me and I'm suggesting to you that every time you tell this story you say something different. You've signed the 1994 statement as being correct, haven't you? You've signed -- you admitted it's your signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another area and I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, moving to another area, you were asked by the Prosecution on Thursday if you were treated as a prisoner of war, whether you were asked your name, rank, and serial number. Now, the people who interviewed you didn't say to you, did they, "You are a prisoner of war," and ask you those details, did they? They just asked you normal questions about who you were.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. They asked me if I was a soldier, what my rank was, which army I belonged to, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: They didn't say, "You're a prisoner of war and you must tell us your name, rank, and serial number," did they?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't say that I was a prisoner of war, or at least I don't remember. As for the rank and serial number, yes, they did say that. They asked me the number of my military post, what sort of soldier I was, and which rank I held.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, you weren't a prisoner of war at all, were you, because you were a civilian, as far as you were concerned.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in war, even a civilian is a prisoner of war. If you have a war going on, everyone who is taken prisoner is a prisoner of war. That at least is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: My point is this: You told them, didn't you, that you were a civilian, not that you were a member of the RS army. If we can just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And this was, as far as you could tell, a civilian police operation, wasn't it? You were in the civilian SUP, and it was the civilian police who were questioning you.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the person who you called the chief telling you that one of the people present during your interview was a Croat and one was from the international community?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did say, but I'm not absolutely positive, therefore I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: It's in your 2000 statement that you recollect the chief telling you that. So is that right that you recalled the chief telling you that one of the people there was a Croat and one from the international community? Does that ring any bell or is that a figment of Ms. Gilleece's imagination?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember. I'll say again, I'm not positive. I believe, as I said a moment ago, the chief explained it to me that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask the 2000 statement of this witness to be given an exhibit number. Not for the truth of its contents, obviously, but to illustrate these contradictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No objection from our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that statement, statement of the witness to the Office of the Prosecution, dated -- again could I have the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's 23-25 May, 2000. The ERN is 02030464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is being admitted into evidence for the purpose indicated by Mr. Jones and solely for that purpose and is being marked as Defence exhibit D161.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I probably didn't need to say that but--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not precluded from making the same point on other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Thursday that you were only beaten at night, I think, and that nobody touched you during the day. So is that right, that all beatings were done under cover of night?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By day they would only beat us in the hall on our way to the lavatory.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And it wasn't every night, was it, that you were beaten, as it was suggested to you. You told us --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. When Cude was on duty, that's when they didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, I asked you on Friday whether you were beaten before you arrived at the SUP, and you said that you were but that didn't leave any marks. Now, I want to look briefly at what you said in your statement, your 2000 statement, and it's page 4 in English, 02030467, third paragraph, starting with the second sentence, and I'll leave out irrelevant parts. "As we walked, Rifet and the other Muslim soldier --" which is referring to Beli -- "would hit one of us which caused us to fall down many times. They hit us with their rifles and they continued to kick us while we walked." Then skipping a paragraph: "We walked for more than two hours to reach Zulfo's house. We stayed outside the house for more than an hour. While we were there three Muslim soldiers in camouflage uniforms and Beli, FNU LNU, beat us with their feet, cursed us, and hit us with their rifles." So for an hour outside that house, three soldiers were beating you with their rifles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for an hour. It lasted perhaps several minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That was a pretty savage beating then, in any event, three soldiers hitting you with their rifles.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, depending on your point of view. They kicked us and hit us with rifle butts. There were three of us taking the beating. If there had only been one person, perhaps the person would have been killed. There were three of us. They kept beating us for several minutes. It certainly wasn't for one hour, and I don't think I ever stated that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's fine. That might have been my inference. But you say that that didn't -- that beating didn't leave any visible marks on your body?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I noticed. It did hurt and probably there were marks, but I simply didn't notice. I did notice the pain, though.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Then you were beaten again, a third time - this is all the time before you arrive in the SUP - during the drive in the back of a truck. And I'm referring to that next paragraph on that page, 4 of 12. "They put us on the floor of the back of a truck. We drove approximately one hour, from what I remember. During the drive, the soldiers began kicking and beating us. They ripped my shirt off and beat me. They also took my wristwatch and my shoes." So again, are you saying that occurred, kicking and a beating, and again that you arrived in the SUP without any marks on your body from that mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I felt pain, but there were no marks on my face because they didn't hit us on our faces. They hit us on our chests and backs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: There may be -- there may be a difference in language when you say that you were beaten or that you suffered beatings. When you use that phrase, do you sometimes use it just to mean being struck but not necessarily referring to severe or hard blows?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say "hard blows," that would mean, for example, if someone knocked me off my feet and I fell on the ground. The blows that they dealt us, they weren't really horrible. Sometimes they kicked us, sometimes they hit us with rifle butts. If the beating had been any harder, none of us would probably have survived in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: But when you -- when you say beating or beaten, are you sometimes referring to something which is nothing more than a slap? I'm not saying that the whole treatment is nothing more but a slap but --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slap. It was a good deal more than that. Being struck several times, not just slapped once.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I think it's the difference between "tuklisu" and "udaralisu" in your language. Actually, that will be difficult to put that question to him.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My language?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That's all right. Moving to another question. Isn't it the fact that there was a lot of violence at that time so that people would often get badly beaten up by the people who first arrested them, by the enemy, especially in this situation, local Muslims angered at being sacked from their mine and chased from their homes? Is that something that you'd accept?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local population not beating us, is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: When you were arrested on the 24th, you mostly recognised local Muslims, didn't you, from Djile and other local villages?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Those people, you accepted, had left their homes sometime before. They'd been --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And weren't a lot of those people angry and aggressive towards you, a Serb, because of this local -- these local occurrences?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And doesn't that explain there was a great deal of violence at the time upon -- upon the arrest of people like yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, when Sarac and Bankovic arrived at the SUP, they had signs of being beaten on them, didn't they, i.e., beaten upon arrest and before they were brought to the prison?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It was night. I can't remember. Bankovic did not have any marks for sure, and I don't remember about Sarac.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, just on the same theme but skipping forward to the day of your exchange. You were emphatic here on Friday that you were never beaten at Potocari. You said, and it's at page 29, lines 1 to 2: "At Potocari no one beat us. I deny that. I'm not sure who stated that in the first place." And I put it to you that you said it in the first place, in your 1994 statement, at page 7 for the record ERN 03602058, second to last sentence, and stated there: "When we arrived in Potocari and parked in front of a house, local inhabitants gathered around us and also beat us and mistreated us." Is it right that you didn't say that either? You never said to an investigator that you were beaten at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having said that to the investigators. You're talking about 1994, aren't you? I don't remember that. As I've said awhile ago, I don't remember that statement at all. I don't remember when I signed it or who asked me questions, but we certainly were not beaten at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And you personally didn't need to go to hospital on the night of your release, on the 16th of October, 1992, did you? You stayed in the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I refused to go to the Zvornik hospital. I spent the night right there. I went to Milici, my own village, there was a hospital there, and I was in a position to receive treatment there.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And you exchanged, with the person you've described as the postman from Fakovici and four others, and you were exchanged alive for 20 or so dead Muslims. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four of us; the postman, myself, and another three persons, it is quite true that we were exchanged for 20 dead Muslim bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: We heard on the audiotape last week Rade Bjelanovic saying that the Serbs never got back their people alive. In fact, it's the reverse, isn't it, at least in that exchange; the Serbs got back their people alive and the Muslims only got back their dead. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the tape, at least to the extent that I remember, indicates that this was before the exchange, when Rade Bjelanovic was involved in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, on that day Sarac could walk, didn't he? He didn't have any problems with his legs or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was able to walk, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Nothing dramatic had happened to his legs. They hadn't been damaged or beaten in any way?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean, about him being able to walk on which specific day?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: On the 16th of October, 1992. Sarac didn't have any --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th, yes, he did. We had to hoist him up onto the lorry outside the SUP building, him and Zoran Bankovic. On the 17th, the next day, he remained at the hotel in Bratunac in bed. I don't know because I myself left for Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Jones, I hate interrupting you, but again this is not clear. From what the witness has answered, I'm not clear in my mind whether Mr. Sarac on the 16th, the day of the exchange, could walk, whether he had any problems with his legs or feet --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because he just said the day, they helped him, they hoisted him, and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was Mr. Sarac's condition the day of the release? Could he walk on his own? Did he need help? And if he needed help, why did he need help? Had he sustained any injuries that impeded him from walking on his own or being able to walk on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for being able to walk on that day, I don't know, but he was beaten that morning before we were to be exchanged, and it was probably as a result of that beating that he was dragging his leg behind. And we were pulling him along because he was not able to move on his own unaided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it now, Mr. Jones. So you move to your next question, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Because on Friday, Mr. Radic, you told us that Sarac wasn't beaten on the day of the exchange. So I take it that's wrong. He was in fact beaten on the day of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think counsel might be mischaracterising the testimony. My memory is that it was only Mr. Sikic, the postman, and I believe Mr. Radic who were waiting for other men who remained in the SUP and were beaten again, and then they were brought to the truck. Unless that is a misunderstanding, I would just ask counsel, please lead us in the transcript to where he is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Sellers is correct, or else we go to your next question, Mr. Jones; it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might be rather slow to find that part of the transcript. My recollection certainly is that this witness said that Sarac was not beaten on the day of the exchange. There's no need to -- I'm not seeking to point out a contradiction. If he can confirm simply that Sarac was beaten on the day of the exchange, then that's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was Sarac beaten on the day of the exchange, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who else was beaten on the day of the exchange? Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not beaten. Sarac and Zoran Bankovic were beaten. I believe that's in my statement, and I also said it on Thursday and Friday. They were taken off the truck, beaten in the SUP building, and then we hoisted them back up on the truck, and then we went for that interview. I believe I said it in my testimony on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir, Mr. Radic. So if there is an apparent contradiction, it's now superseded.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: It's that those beatings then occurred after the last time that you saw the person calling himself Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That beating after I saw Mr. Naser Oric -- you mean the beating of Sarac? Yes. That's after the visit of Naser Oric, because we saw Naser Oric on the 25th, and this happened on the 26th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: That might be wrong. It would be the 15th and the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15th and 16th, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: So Sarac was beaten after you last saw the person calling himself Naser Oric. I want to be absolutely --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16th.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... step-by-step. You last saw Naser Oric on the 15th of October; correct? The eve of the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Sarac was beaten on the 16th of October.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's so.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, going back to that -- that visit or that meeting on the eve of the exchange, on the 15th of October, when you told us you saw Naser Oric, you say that you were taken to Naser's office and that he asked Sarac questions and then struck him. And I'm going to refer to your 2000 statement, page 10 of 12, ERN 02030473, and you say that Naser asked Veselin Sarac about Akif, and then you say, "Naser Oric then began kicking Sarac and beating him." Now, just stopping there firstly, that's not true, is it, because here you told us it was one strike with the back of the hand. That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly hit him with his hand. Whether it was a fist or the palm of his hand, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... hit Sarac, did he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until then, but this time he probably angered him by not acknowledging that he knew Akif, and he told us later that he did know Akif, and Naser was probably upset over that, angered, and he hit him.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Sir, you don't need to retell the whole story. I've got specific questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is basically what we want to know, Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I ask my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, and get it over and done with because you are inviting answers that are at a tangent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm inviting them. I'm getting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're getting them but you're also inviting them. So let's try to restrict the questions to what is basic and essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: In your 2000 statement, Mr. Radic, which you signed as true, you said that Oric was kicking Sarac. My point is that's not true, is it? He was not kicking Sarac.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once he hit him with his hand and then with his foot --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is simple --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please allow the witness to continue, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish answering your question. Because you interrupted. The moment he said he moved from the hit to the foot, you intervened yourself. So please answer the question, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A simple yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a simple yes answer because the moment he started answering your question, you interrupted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because it only required a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but -- that's what you think. Did Mr. -- the man or the person you describe as Naser Oric, or the person who described himself as Naser Oric, hit Veselin Sarac by hand only or also by foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he hit him with his hand and then later he laid us down on his arm, and then he did something with his leg. He sort of slid his leg up -- up the man's body and did I don't know what, and then he released him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jones, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's not kicking, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Precisely. If you go to the previous page - this is why I intervened - because I'm usually careful for every word that the witness is saying. If you go to page 66, line 23 -- or line 21, the witness is saying in line 21: "He certainly hit him with his hand. Whether it was the fist or the palm of his hand, I have no idea." Then you intervened and you suggested he hit Sarac, didn't he? And he said, not until then. Not until then. And this is why I was on the watch-out and the look-out for your next questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That answered to me not before then, the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was one moment where he just hit him with his hands but then there were other moments that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me take it this way, Your Honour, and I'm going to skip ahead and then skip back.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You told us on Friday -- sorry. Let me find the exact quote. You told us you don't know -- you didn't know whether the person who called himself Naser hit Sarac on the head or on the body, and you said and I'll quote, it's from the 14th of January, Friday, page 6, lines 20 to 24: Question: "So did Mr. Naser Oric strike Veselin on his face or on his chest or on another part of his body?" Answer: "I didn't notice because I wasn't really paying any attention. In fact I didn't dare to look. I think he struck him on the face. I'm not sure." Now, doesn't it follow that you didn't actually see the contact, because if you saw the contact, you would know whether he struck him on the head or on the body?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the face. I think that's what I said on Friday as well.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: No. You didn't say that. You said, "I didn't dare to look."

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You didn't actually see the contact. You weren't looking.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said he struck him on the face. I didn't dare to look openly. I kept my eyes more on the ground than -- than I looked sideways.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you kept your eyes on the ground, so in fact you didn't see the contact at all, did you, and that's why you don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also said he looked sideways. You took advantage of one part of his statement and forgot or ignored the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's being clear. He didn't look -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. blatantly look, but he saw what was happening. This is what he's telling us now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And he's told us he didn't see whether it was to the head or to the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's let him answer, not you.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You don't know, do you, whether the hit was to the head or to the body, do you, for sure?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe it was on the head, as far as I was able to see. If I were certain 100 per cent, I would tell you. But I could see the movement of his hand and where it was directed, and it was moving towards the face.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: All right. Now you said that this followed a conversation between Naser, the person calling himself Naser, and Sarac about Akif. And you said, and this is in your 2000 statement, that you heard Oric say to Sarac: "His, Akif's, father was a butcher. You should know. He is my nephew, my sister's son." Now, on Friday you said it wasn't nephew, it was uncle which you heard. But it's very specific, though, isn't it, in your 2000 statement; sister's son, i.e., nephew. So haven't you changed that part of your story, too, in light of what you've heard subsequently?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my language you say "ujak," which means "uncle," to denote the brother of your mother. That's what I believe I said.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You told us that you learned later that Akif was, as you say, the uncle of Naser. I'm looking at Friday's hearing at page 9, lines 18 to 22: "Among those dead bodies there was also the body of Akif Hrustic. I apologise I believe the last name is Hrustic. This is something I found out later. I found out that he was the uncle of Mr. Naser Oric. At least, that's what I heard. I have no idea whether it's true or not, but that's what I heard." Now, my suggestion to you, and if you'll let me put it in stages, is firstly that you heard no such conversation about nephews or uncles on the 15th of October, 1992, that you later heard, probably from a Serb, that Akif was Naser's nephew or uncle, and you added that to your 2000 statement that you heard that conversation, although it wasn't true, and then later, perhaps when someone told you that Akif was 20 years older than Naser and was not his nephew or uncle, you changed your story again. That's my suggestion to you, that you're adding to the story --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again I think you have to split it in two parts, because as it is it will only confuse the witness, and I wouldn't even let him answer your question because I wouldn't know which part of the question he would be answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's take it one by one. The first question -- the first part is that you're suggesting that you never -- that he never heard any such conversation about nephews or uncles on the 15th of October, 1992. Is that correct? He's suggesting to you, Mr. Jones, that when you heard this conversation about Akif Hrustic being an uncle or nephew, whatever, you were not telling us the truth; you never heard any such conversation on the 15th of October, 1992, or on any other date for that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naser did ask Sarac, How could you possibly not know Hrustic, because his father was -- I'm not sure now whether he said butcher or barber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's being suggested to you that you never heard this conversation, your answer is no, I did hear that conversation. That is your answer. Okay. Your next question now, Mr. Jones, once you have got this confirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time it's true that you heard or you say you found out later that Akif Hrustic was Mr. Oric's uncle? Is that true, that you found that out later?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, uncle or nephew. I don't know exactly what -- which.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because at the end of the day where is it getting you? I mean this part, particular, whether he was the uncle or nephew --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's neither, he's not uncle or nephew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. You should know better about that, but in any case, let's move.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And watch the clock because you've got roughly 15 minutes from now, and you choose the time when you would like to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about the radio, the conversation you heard of an exchange on the radio. Now, firstly, in your 2000 statement to investigators, or indeed in any prior statement, you never mentioned that Sarac left the prison to go and speak on the radio, did you? It's not something you've ever mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me about that. There were no such questions. I provided only information in response to specific questions.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You never mentioned, did you, before that Sarac left the SUP to dispose of Kukic's body? That's something you spoke of for the first time when you came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's in the statement, my statement. I think there is reference to the time when Sarac left the building with Kukic's body.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Your 2000 statement to the ICTY investigators, you think you said it there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they asked me the question, then it's there. If they didn't, then it's natural that I didn't talk about things that the investigator didn't ask about. But it should be there. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: It would have been -- even if not asked, if would have been an important detail to volunteer that information, wouldn't it, that Sarac left the prison to dispose of a body?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you if they didn't ask me, it's possible that I didn't say it because if I were to talk about everything that happened every minute over those 20-something days, 21 days that I spent imprisoned, it would take a month.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, for this radio, this conversation on the radio, you weren't present for that, for that conversation, were you, where we heard a voice purporting to be Sarac's?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Sarac's voice.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You weren't there, were you? You weren't present when he spoke on the radio.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I was supposed to be there, but I wasn't. I heard it later on the tape. The mix-up they made, they confused me with Bjelanovic's uncle. So I didn't go, Sarac went. But I could tell, I could identify the voice.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: In the past ten or so years before you came to The Hague and heard that tape, you haven't been asked to identify his voice, have you, at any time in the past ten years?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: The first time that you heard that tape and claimed to identify the voice of Sarac was when you came to The Hague on this occasion, wasn't it, some 12 years after events?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Just two questions regarding the content of that interview. We heard reference to Cerska. Cerska was in Muslim hands throughout all of 1992, wasn't it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And we also heard reference to a Branko Sekulic, but he was never imprisoned with you, was he?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then just before the break, we'd like to introduce in evidence with regard to authenticity of the tape the IIF form which was disclosed to us, which indicates that the tape has not been authenticated that it's not an original, that it was received from the RS state security service through the RS bureau of cooperation, and the originator is the famous Daj Milutic [phoen] of the RS bureau of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would also like to remind the Trial Chamber, as the Trial Chamber stated before, that when it is stated there is not an original on the IIF or the MIF meaning that it might be a copy, I think we've had this discussion about copies and questions whether they were originals or not, and I would just ask Counsellor to refrain from characterising people the infamous or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I said "famous."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- the famous, whatever that might mean, either directly or indirectly. We would also not oppose Counsellor presenting this document but we would like to make those statements concerning it and that it is a work product of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken, Ms. Sellers. And also, Mr. Jones, when we say "point taken," it also relates to comments that sometimes are passed and shouldn't be passed about persons who are not present here. And in any case, such comments ought to be avoided in the presence of the witnesses. Should we take the break now or do you want to proceed with further questions? This is D161.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll take the break now, and my apologies at my attempt at levity. It wasn't meant in anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Basically, we will be resuming at roughly ten to one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the last document that relates to the audiotape mentioned by Mr. Jones earlier on should have been D162 and not 161, the reason being that it was the 2000 witness statement which is 161. Correct? So my mistake. D161 for this document should read D162. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you, Mr. Wubben. I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next projected witness is Mr. Branimir Mitrovic. He is waiting, but it's now already past 1.00. Is it possible to make an inquiry as to whether he shall give testimony today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I should have actually asked Mr. Jones, but I took it that if he didn't mention anything, the idea was to finish this witness and there be enough time for the other one to start, no? That's how I took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly from my point of view I can be finished in, I think, ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I gathered, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it depends very much on Your Honours and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, for the Prosecution it is also around 15 minutes. That will bring us past half past one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then send -- I don't know if you want to start. It's up to you. We are here to work. So it's up to you. If you want to send him back to the hotel and we start him tomorrow, we start him tomorrow. But we have 15 minutes left and you want to use those 15 minutes, we use them. I don't know. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will certainly then use those 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I wouldn't like is that we end up with not being able to even bring him in, which I would still require to do if we come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm supported by this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, not lose more time. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I can proceed quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you were shown a video, it's P98, on Friday, with an interview with Mr. Sarac and yourself and Nevenko. You were all interviewed together, weren't you, so you could all hear what each other was saying?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed, you were tired and disoriented, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to say, I didn't even see the camera, and I had never seen this footage before, before I arrived here in The Hague. I saw a man holding the microphone but not a camera. I'm not sure where this footage was taken, at the hotel in Bratunac or elsewhere, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Well, let's stick with when you were interviewed when you were first exchanged on the 16th of October. On that occasion you were tired and disoriented, weren't you, when you were interviewed? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Did the people who interviewed you offer you medical assistance before being interviewed? Did they give you that option?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you later found out that the statement or the -- the statement was taken by a journalist. I'm reading from Friday's transcript, page 10, lines 14 to 16: "Yes, there was a man there I didn't know. I later found out that he was a journalist. He put a mike in front of me, a microphone or whatever." Did you find out that the person who interviewed you was a Mr. Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Who interviewed you, if you remember the name?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name at all. The man didn't introduce himself. At least, to the best of my recollection that was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Why do you say that you found out later that he was a journalist if you don't know who he was? What actually did you learn?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew even back then that he was a journalist, but I didn't know the person's name. He was carrying a microphone around so of course he was a journalist, but I what I did not see were the cameras that were taking the footage.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, he wasn't the only person there in the room there with you three, was there? At one point we heard Mr. Sarac say, "Why are there so many people now?" Is it right that there were lots of other people, at least at one point, in the room with you when you were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that Mr. Sarac said that there were that many people around. This is not something that I noticed while watching the tape in that room at the hotel. But there weren't that many people. There were the four of us, five including the postman who had been exchanged, there was another lady, and this journalist; no one else.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I won't pursue it with you, Mr. Radic, but it's in -- I refer to the transcript where that's stated, why there's so many people now. Now, did the interviewer prompt you personally and give you information that, for example, Kemo's surname was Ahmetovic and that he was from Pale? He told you that, didn't he? I'm looking at page 6 of the transcript. You mention Kemo and he said, "All right. We have the details, Ahmetovic." Isn't that right, that he told you who Kemo was?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that he told me. This was maybe stated by Sarac. I remember that the person's name was Kemal Ahmetovic, called Kemo, from Pale. I found out after I had been exchanged. It was perhaps three or four days later that Mr. Bjelanovic, the chief, told me who the person was.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: The interviewer said after that -- or before, "We have the details." Now, isn't it right that in fact this wasn't a journalist; you were being debriefed by the Serb security services? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to be to be quite honest, I don't know. What we were told is that he was a journalist. I personally did not know the person to know who they were. It may as well have been the Serbian intelligence services, but I can't be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I want to play just a couple of very short segments of that video. And we need to switch the booth for the Defence mode. And I'm going to show -- it's a portion where Mr. Sarac is being interviewed, and it's just before and after he mentions Naser. So if we can play that. We don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We don't seem to have sound. Well, we might need to come back to that because there are a couple of clips which we will need the sound for. Your Honour, perhaps I might -- this may be a technical problem which we'll have to come back to. It might help to explain two things. The first clip is to show that the tape skips before Mr. Sarac is asked or mentions Naser. It's a point I don't necessarily have to deal with this witness to get him to agree that it skips. It's a point which I can make subsequently. However, at the very end there is something which this witness says and we will need to hear that. What I could do is carry on with some other questions and then come back. Perhaps the technical booth would have solved the problem in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately, we just have that in B/C/S, not in English. But I don't know if you followed what was being said there, Mr. Radic. I'd ask you whether you agree that before Mr. Sarac mentions Naser, the video skips. We can play it again now.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Do you agree that Mr. Sarac says something to the effect of "So much for now and you can ask more further." The interviewer says, "So that means --" and then there are skips and then the interviewer says something else and then Sarac refers to "Naser hitting me here."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I ask counsel just to point us to the transcript, exactly what it's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, in fact it's marked on the transcript, page 3, second line from the bottom. Interviewer: "So that means --" cut. So I think it's accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: My question is and it may be that you can't help with this, but do you know what the interviewer said, if anything, to prompt Sarac to mention Naser? Is there anything which you recall the interviewer saying which doesn't appear on that video? Did the interviewer say something like, "Did you see Naser Oric?" Something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, believe me, I don't remember. I didn't even see a camera.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: I'm just going to play now a final segment, and this is yourself being interviewed, and it's at the very end of the tape, and just for everyone's benefit, on the transcript it's page 6, and the interviewer says, "And where was this? Do you remember anybody else among them that you knew from before and who ..." I'm going to play that last segment and see if the witness agrees that he says no or gives a negative answer. If we could play that.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Do you agree that you were asked there by the interviewer whether you were remember anybody else from the prison and that you were replying no? We can replay that segment. It might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Do you hear yourself saying "ne" there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this in reference to us, the prisoners, or to the Muslim gentlemen? What is this in reference to, did I know anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: My question is, watching that video, did you hear the interviewer saying, "Do you remember anybody else among them that you knew from before, and who?" And then you were replying in the negative. And we don't know necessarily what was meant, but that you were replying no. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably agree. I'm not sure what this is about.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Well, isn't it right that when interviewed you didn't say, when asked whether you knew anyone, "Well, yes, there was Naser Oric, the commander of the Srebrenica forces. I saw him three times." You didn't say any of that, did you, when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: It's the sort of thing you would have mentioned or certain thing -- let me put it differently. You would remember, wouldn't you, if you had said that to the interviewer, mentioned encounters with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three encounters, yes. That's what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Yes, but my point was that it wasn't to the interviewer, but I'll move on from that subject, and we may ask for the transcript of P98.1E to be corrected to reflect the last -- not now, but on a subsequent occasion. Now, a final couple of questions, Mr. Radic. In July 1992, before you were captured, weren't you brought into a police station for acting violently in a health centre and cautioned?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which police station; Milici or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Milici.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not even in the hospital. I was back home receiving treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Are you saying on oath categorically that you were never brought into Milici police station for acting violently?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on what grounds.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: My question is: Did that ever happen? Surely you would remember if you were brought into Milici police station.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen several times before the war, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: In July 1992, which is not before the war, were you brought into the police station in Milici?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's possible, though.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Radic, you've given us details here of conversations and how people looked, et cetera. Surely your memory is good enough to remember whether you were brought into a police station and cautioned for acting violently.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who my acting violently was directed against. If you bring that up, perhaps it will be easier for me to remember the specific instance.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Are you often brought into police stations, Mr. Radic? I mean, surely you can remember if you were brought in in July 1992. That's what I'm asking you, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often, that is not the case. I was not often brought into police stations. It was maybe two or three times before the war for minor infractions. During the war it's possible that I was brought in. It's possible, I say, but I can't remember. It's as simple as that. I refused to go to the mine. I know I was brought in by the police once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a new document which will be a Defence exhibit. It's a report to the police station commander Milici dated 7th July, 1992. And it's ERN 01782331.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: You'll be shown a copy of that document in B/C/S. Now, according to that document, Mr. Radic, and take your time. According to that document, a female doctor reported that Nedjelko Radic, and you told us you were the only one in Milici, was disturbing patients at the health centre, making threats and firing a rifle. Making threats, that is, to patients, the wounded and sick, and he was brought into the police station and cautioned for it. Do you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're looking at the same document, I just want to know where is counsel seeing that he was making threats to patients on the document? I would not necessarily that it is true but it does say making threats and firing a rifle. It doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Disturbing patients, making threats and firing a rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radic, do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would I fire a rifle? It says "making threats with a stick."

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Okay. Apparently the translation might have been wrong. It says in this document, what we have: "Nedjelko Radic was disturbing patients at the health centre, making threats and firing a rifle. The above mentioned was brought into the SM police station and warned, cautioned." So my question is, is that correct, that in July 1992 you were brought into the police station for that incident?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I know that once I refused an order to go to the mine. I do remember that, but not this. Why would I have been firing at patients? This is totally insane.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Never mind why you would be doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I mean he just doesn't remember, so let's -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's something one would remember, that's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just leave that to us to decide. He's telling you I don't remember, I don't remember. And what I don't understand, whether it was a rifle or stick, because someone mentioned a stick.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, it's a rifle in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but in the Bosnian -- B/C/S, what is it? "Pusko" is what, a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That I can't help you with.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is very specific. "Made threats and fired a rifle," that's what it says. There is no reference whatsoever to any wooden stick or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness is saying he doesn't remember such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll finally try to remind or jog the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Could it be these patients were in fact wounded Muslims, wounded in ethnic cleansing operations, probably from Nurici, Sadici, Kratine and Toljina [phoen] and that you went and threatened them and fired your rifle at them because they were Muslims and because of an animosity which you have toward Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no Muslims at the Milici hospital at that time. At least, that's what I remember. How would I have been allowed to enter a hospital carrying a rifle, in the first place, to fire at patients? There was security there, police. They would not have allowed me to enter a hospital carrying a weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Does the name Hasim Becirovic, son of Ralf [phoen], from Polem Besici [phoen] familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELKO RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: He and his brother were taken to the health centre around that time and never seen again. Has that got anything to do with you going there and discharging a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I will object. I mean, I think we've taken a big leap from making threats to someone disappearing out of a hospital because someone was there making threats. I would ask counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, and this is my final question, and you will no doubt disagree but I put it to you nonetheless, is that this did occur and that you had no compunction, back then, about threatening wounded and sick Muslims in a hospital and that you have no compunction about saying falsehoods to this Tribunal in order to get Oric, another Muslim, indeed a symbol of Srebrenica's Muslims, in trouble before this Tribunal, and that you've told so many untruths you can no longer keep track of them. That's my suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would state that it appears the witness is having a bit of difficulty answering what appears to have been possibly a statement and not question. If counsel has a question, might we have that more directly put?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will put the question myself. It's been put to you, Mr. Radic, that you have been consistently lying to us, knowingly lying to us, simply because you want to see Mr. Oric, Naser Oric, convicted and sentenced by this Tribunal. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would never have Mr. Naser Oric convicted if it were up to me. If it were up to me, I would set him free right now and I would dearly like to see Kemo in Mr. Naser's place. I was never in favour of anything like that in relation to any person, including Naser Oric. Naser Oric never caused me any harm. That's all I can say. I definitely disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE SERB AUTHORITIES OR
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I should ask for that last document to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will being given Exhibit number D163. Now we have 15 minutes, 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keeping in mind that we have got two questions, Ms. Sellers, and I would also need a couple of minutes to explain to the next witness why we kept him here waiting without even letting him in the courtroom. So do you think you can finish in less than 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try my very best.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
